failure_modes: Mucin- or excipient-stabilized soluble complexes resist detergent/protease under the chosen conditions and mimic membrane protection, producing false-positive protected-activity results (supports competing explanation).

Spike-in tracer and capture reagents behave differently from endogenous EVs in mucin/device matrices (spike-in validates assay performance while endogenous EVs are absent or lost), so spike-in recovery masks true absence of protected endogenous material.
Low biomass of bounded fractions forces assay compromises (dilution, pooling, or limited replicates) producing irreproducible or uninterpretable co-localization and activity readouts across lots.

Capture reagents non‑specifically bind non‑vesicular particulate material (mucin aggregates, protein complexes, cell debris) that co-fractionates with particle peaks, creating co-localized capture signal unlinked to EVs.
Detergent/protease/RNase conditions chosen fail to fully disrupt the particular non‑vesicular complexes present (or conversely disrupt EVs incompletely), producing ambiguous protection readouts.
Particle-counting methods (NTA/TRPS) detect non-EV particulates from device/mucin matrices and report particle peaks that are not EVs, misleading co-localization metrics.

Even if protected endogenous activity is correctly assigned to EVs in vitro, species- and administration-route specific barriers (e.g., mucociliary clearance demonstrated in NHPs) prevent in vivo brain delivery, so the gate would not predict translational delivery (consistent with macaque negative biodistribution).

Prequalification/compatibility gaps for capture reagents or buffers with mucin and device rinse solutions prevent consistent spike-in recovery, producing inconclusive assay validation (falsely qualifying or rejecting lots).
strongest_objection: The experiment can produce a reproducible, assay-validated ‘‘protected’’ signal that nevertheless does not prove the activity is carried by bona fide EVs because mucin, device-derived debris, or other non‑vesicular complexes present after simulated nasal passage can (A) stabilize or shield soluble bioactives from detergent/protease/RNase and (B) co‑isolate with particle-like counts and capture reagents, yielding spike-in‑compatible recovery but a false-positive protected‑activity readout. This would lead to adopting an identity+potency gate that selects material with artifactual ‘‘membrane-protected’’ activity that will not predict in vivo delivery or mechanism and could misdirect bridging and manufacturing decisions.
